canonical_statement: The primary study aim was to evaluate the relationship between UFH anti-Xa activity and thromboelastography reaction time in critically ill adults with COVID-19 receiving therapeutic UFH infusions.
Secondary aims included evaluating the relationship between aPTT and TEG reaction time and describing clinically relevant bleeding, thromboembolic events, and other clinical outcomes.
The study was a single-center retrospective cohort conducted at Banner University Medical Center Phoenix over March 1, 2020 through May 31, 2021.

Inclusion required age at least 18 years, ICU admission, SARS-CoV-2 RNA detected by nasopharyngeal swab, continuous-infusion therapeutic UFH for at least 24 hours, and concurrent standard TEG and anti-Xa measurements obtained within 2 hours of each other.

population.label: Patients eligible for the retrospective cohort
inclusion_criteria: SARS-CoV-2 RNA detected by nasopharyngeal swab
Concurrent standard TEG and anti-Xa obtained within <=2 hours of each other

canonical_statement: Patients receiving continuous-infusion UFH during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation were excluded.

population.label: Patients screened for study inclusion
exclusion_criteria: Continuous-infusion UFH during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation

canonical_statement: Standard TEG testing used the TEG 5000 system with citrated whole blood collected from indwelling arterial or venous lines, kaolin activation, and calcium chloride recalcification.
Therapeutic-intensity continuous-infusion UFH was used in the ICU cohort, and initiation in patients without known VTE was at the attending physician's discretion.

exposures.details: Initiation could occur with or without known VTE at attending physician discretion

canonical_statement: TEG use during UFH infusions was at the attending physician's discretion, and no standardized protocol guided UFH infusion dosing based on TEG findings.

During the study period, clinicians could target the upper therapeutic anti-Xa range of 0.5-0.7 units/mL when respiratory status decompensated or TEG suggested persistent hypercoagulability despite therapeutic anti-Xa; this institutional practice later ceased after publication of a landmark ICU COVID-19 anticoagulation trial.
Patients were followed for up to the first 10 concurrent TEG and anti-Xa assessments meeting study criteria, or until UFH was discontinued, death occurred, or discharge occurred.
Ancillary laboratory values used in analyses were taken from the same patient day as the paired TEG and anti-Xa assessments but were not required to fall within the same 2-hour pairing window.
The coagulation index was calculated as -0.2454(R time) + 0.0184(K time) + 0.1655(MA) - 0.0241(alpha angle) - 5.0220.
The institutional UFH anti-Xa therapeutic range was 0.3-0.7 units/mL; values below 0.3 units/mL were subtherapeutic and values above 0.7 units/mL were supratherapeutic.

outcome.definition: Therapeutic 0.3-0.7 units/mL; subtherapeutic <0.3 units/mL; supratherapeutic >0.7 units/mL

canonical_statement: TEG reaction time was categorized as therapeutic at 9-13 minutes, subtherapeutic below 9 minutes, and supratherapeutic above 13 minutes.

outcome.definition: Therapeutic 9-13 min; subtherapeutic <9 min; supratherapeutic >13 min

canonical_statement: Confirmed venous thromboembolic events required positive computed tomography or ultrasound findings.

outcome.definition: Positive computed tomography or ultrasound finding

canonical_statement: Clinically relevant bleeding was defined as known or suspected bleeding that necessitated UFH interruption and was documented in a physician progress note.

outcome.definition: Known or suspected bleeding necessitating UFH interruption and documented in a physician progress note

canonical_statement: The primary endpoint was the correlation coefficient between standard TEG reaction time and UFH anti-Xa concentration; secondary clinical endpoints included bleeding, thromboembolic events, mechanical ventilation duration, ICU and hospital length of stay, and in-hospital mortality.

Pearson correlation coefficients were used for continuous associations, therapeutic-category agreement was assessed with kappa-based agreement analysis, and group comparisons used t tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for continuous data and chi-square or Fisher exact tests for dichotomous data.
Multivariable analysis for bleeding or thromboembolic-event risk factors was not performed because few covariates were associated with either outcome on univariable analysis.
Of 884 patients identified as receiving continuous-infusion UFH during the study period, 237 met inclusion criteria and contributed 413 concurrent TEG and anti-Xa laboratory assessments.

canonical_statement: The retrospective design limited reliable ascertainment of clinical outcomes, particularly bleeding and attribution of bleeding to UFH versus other causes.
The study definition of clinically relevant bleeding and inconsistent documentation prevented reliable classification of bleeding severity as major or minor.
Confirmed thromboembolic events may be affected by selection bias because diagnostic imaging was likely performed primarily when clinical suspicion was present.
Physician discretion in ordering TEG may have selected higher-risk or clinically discordant patients and therefore limits generalizability of the observed anti-Xa/TEG relationships.
TEG and anti-Xa measurements were permitted to be up to 2 hours apart, with an average separation of approximately 1 hour, which could reduce the accuracy of correlation estimates.
The 9-13 minute TEG reaction-time range used to define therapeutic UFH effect was considered exploratory and may not represent a validated therapeutic threshold.
The lower anti-Xa values observed in patients with clinically relevant bleeding may have been influenced by anti-Xa sampling after UFH had already been stopped for suspected bleeding.
The authors concluded that overall correlation between TEG reaction time and anti-Xa activity was low and that therapeutic anti-Xa values frequently disagreed with TEG reaction-time categories.
The authors concluded that routine TEG use to assist UFH dosing in critically ill patients with COVID-19 remains inconclusive.
The authors stated that further research is needed to evaluate TEG-based anticoagulation dosing and decision-making in severely ill patients with COVID-19.
